etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English than, thanne, from Old English þanne, a variant of þonne (“then, since, because”), from Proto-West Germanic *þan, from Proto-Germanic *þan (“at that, at that time, then”), from earlier *þam, from Proto-Indo-European *tóm, accusative masculine of *só (“demonstrative pronoun, that”).

Cognate with Dutch dan (“than”), German denn (“than”), German dann (“then”). Doublet of then.

definitions.definition: Used in comparisons, to introduce the basis of comparison.

quote.citation: 2013 July 20, “Old Soldiers?”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8845:
quote.text: Whether modern, industrial man is less or more warlike than his hunter-gatherer ancestors is impossible to determine. The machine gun is so much more lethal than the bow and arrow that comparisons are meaningless.

quote.citation: 1665, Edward Stillingfleet, William Laud, Thomas Carwell, A Rational Account of the Grounds of Protestant Religion:
quote.text: Answer me if you can, any other way, than because the Scriptures, which are infallible, Say so.

definitions.definition: (obsolete outside dialects, usually used with for) Because; for.

quote.text: If thou say yes, then puttest thou on Christ (that is, the wisdome of God, the Father) unkunning, unpower, or euil will: for than he could not make his rule so good as an other did his.

quote.citation: 1668, William Lawson, A Way to Get Wealth:
quote.text: You shall also take the fine earth or mould which is found in the hollow of old Willow trees, rising from the root almost to the middle of the Tree, at least so far as the tree is hollow, for than this, there is no earth or mould finer or richer.

definitions.definition: introduces a comparison, and is associated with comparatives, and with words such as more, less, and fewer. Typically, it seeks to measure the force of an adjective or similar description between two predicates.
(now chiefly dialectal or a misspelling) At that time; then.
